ch:0: This is DOMA, the Collings CRM, rebuilt with GeeVee. Every page of the current CRM is here, on one record. The difference is GeeVee. It listens to the agent's calls and recaps, and does the work that follows: booking, drafting, filing, chasing, reporting. Anything that leaves the office, a text, an email, a document, a listing, waits for the agent to tap approve. Five chapters, about ten minutes. Chapter one. A call becomes a listing. A seller lead has come in from Facebook. The rule at Collings is simple: a new seller lead is always a call from the agent, inside twenty four hours. GeeVee never messages them first. Watch what one call does.
ch:1: Chapter two. Live by Saturday. Outside suppliers get a booking email they confirm from. Publishing leaves the office, so it sits behind the Victorian checklist and a protected approval. And the street hears about the listing the day it goes live.
ch:2: Chapter three. Saturday to sold. From the open home to the signed contract, nobody fills in a form. Buyers are ranked, offers are recorded from calls, the contract is filled from the result.
ch:3: Chapter four. The money. Where the agent lands this year, what closes the gap, and a database that works itself.
ch:4: Chapter five. The office. Where the week is leaking money, by agent, before it costs anything. And the end of the day in one tap.
st:0: This is Today. The only list an agent needs. Everything GeeVee has prepared sits here in order: offers first, then replies, calls and approvals. Each card is a decision, not a form. The written offer is at the top because offers are urgent.
st:1: Helen Vu enquired overnight. The clock shows the hours left under the twenty four hour rule. The agent calls her from DOMA, so GeeVee hears the call.
st:2: The night before, the appraisal pack is ready to print: comparable sales, price evidence inside the ten percent rule, the marketing plan, the checklist. Nothing was typed to make it.
st:3: After the appraisal, in the car, the agent tells GeeVee what was agreed. Price, commission, method, marketing budget, photo day. That recap is the whole data entry for a listing. GeeVee checks the ten percent price rule and fills in the sales authority.
st:4: Documents to a vendor are protected. They wait on Today until the agent checks and approves. One tap, and it goes to Helen and Mark for electronic signing. GeeVee chases if it is not signed in time.
st:5: This is what the vendor sees on their phone. The moment both sign, GeeVee files the authority, creates the listing, emails the photographer, and drafts the campaign and the Property Price Statement.
st:6: The photographer confirms from the email. After the shoot they deliver from the same link. GeeVee files the photos, picks the hero image, writes the listing copy from the recorded facts, and picks three comparable sales for the price statement.
st:7: Go live runs the Victorian checklist. Signed authority. Price statement with three comparables. Advertised price inside ten percent and not below the estimate. Vendor identity sighted. Photos. Approved copy. Then it waits for the agent. On approval it publishes, books the first open home, and sets the auction with a reserve reminder.
st:8: GeeVee ranks the buyers to call first: offers, enquiries, open home interest, portal views, and whether their finance is ready. An offer heard on a call becomes an offer record with its conditions. Presenting it to the vendor is a protected approval.
st:9: The vendor's decision is dictated. Acceptance fills the Contract of Sale from the offer. Both parties sign on their phones. Sold: the contract is filed, deposit and settlement go in the diary, the sold price task is set under the seven day rule, and the buyers who missed out get a text.
st:10: The forecast shows what is earned, booked and in the pipeline, against the agent's target. The gap becomes a number of appraisals, and a list of the owners most likely to say yes. Today is ordered by expected fee as well as urgency.
st:11: Every owner gets a rhythm: a market update, an anniversary note, a what is it worth now. GeeVee watches for selling signals and turns the strong ones into calls. Touches go only to owners with permission evidence. Do not contact owners get nothing.
st:12: Seven of the same approval is one tap. Delegation is a sentence: ask Priya to call the open home buyers, remind me Friday. If it slips, it comes back to the agent.
st:13: The weekly vendor report is written from the real campaign numbers. When the market says the price is wrong, GeeVee scripts the conversation. That is a call from the agent, never a message.
st:14: Everything GeeVee does, the agent can do by hand. The current CRM asks forty one fields for a listing. This asks nine, in three short steps, and fills the rest from the property database.
st:15: Everything that leaves DOMA is simulated in this prototype. This page is the build list: the phone line and transcription first, then permissions and the audit log, then the gateways, signing and portals.
st:16: Open home day. The buyers who enquired during the week are already on the list. At the door, the agent checks people in on a phone, or they scan the code. When the session closes, every warm buyer gets a text for approval, the vendor gets the numbers, and if two buyers raised the price, the price conversation goes on Today as a call.
st:17: The moment a listing goes live, GeeVee writes to the street. A letter to forty doors, a text to the owners who gave permission, a door knock booked before the open home, and the owners with selling signals put on Today as calls. Every appraisal that comes back is tracked to the listing that started it.
st:18: The principal's page. Seller leads past twenty four hours. Live listings with no activity in a week. Approvals waiting more than a day. Compliance gaps. Slipped tasks. By agent. Every row opens the record, and GeeVee names who to talk to today.
st:19: For an auction the law needs a bidders record and a reserve in writing. Bidders are registered with ID. The reserve letter goes to the vendor to sign. After the result, sold under the hammer flows straight into the contract. Passed in puts the negotiation on Today. No bids puts the vendor debrief on Today as a call.
st:20: The vendor has their own page. Views, enquiries, open home numbers, the next step, documents and reports. Offer amounts never show there. A question from the vendor lands on the agent's Today.
st:21: At five, close the day. What got done, what slipped moves to tomorrow, and tomorrow in order with travel time. Driving mode for the car. Keys for the desk.
sub:1:3: GeeVee is transcribing as they talk.
sub:1:4: GeeVee heard an appraisal for Thursday at two, a co-owner called Mark, a price expectation, and a text the agent promised. Untick anything wrong and save. The appraisal is booked with travel time, the pack is prepared, and the text goes to Today for approval.
sub:3:3: Saved. Internal work is done at once, with undo. The authority is on Today for approval.
sub:5:2: A typed signature, a tick, sign. Then the co-owner.
sub:7:4: All checks passed. Request go-live, then approve it from the bell.
sub:8:1: Jordan Park is first. An offer on an earlier call, open home interest, and finance pre-approved.
sub:16:2: HOT, warm or cold. That one tap decides who gets called tomorrow.
sub:19:6: Sold under the hammer. The contract, the diary and the under-bidders follow on their own.
out:0: What just happened. The appraisal booked from the call, with travel time and the pack ready to print. The sales authority filled in from one dictated recap, approved in one protected tap. Both vendors signed on their phones; the listing, the photographer booking, the campaign and the price statement followed on their own. That was two conversations and eight taps. The agent did not type a form.
out:1: What just happened. Photos filed, hero picked, listing copy written and three comparables chosen when the photographer delivered. The Victorian checklist passed before publishing: authority, price statement, 10% rule, vendor ID. The first open home booked, and 40 neighbours written to with a door knock before it. Photos to portals in one approval, and forty neighbours written to. Every listing becomes the next appraisal.
out:2: What just happened. The week's enquirers pre-registered at the door; the vendor texted the numbers an hour after close. An offer heard on a call recorded with its conditions and presented in writing. Accepted, contract filled and signed, sold; or at auction: bidders record, reserve signed, sold under the hammer, under-bidders texted. No offer form, no contract typed, no buyer forgotten.
out:3: What just happened. The forecast turns the gap to target into a number of appraisals and a ranked list of owners. The database works itself: a rhythm for every owner and a call when a selling signal shows. The vendor sees their own campaign and asks questions without a phone call. Prospecting that happens even on a busy week.
out:4: What just happened. Seller leads past 24 hours, quiet listings, approvals waiting, compliance gaps and slipped tasks, each row opening the record. Seven of the same approval in one tap; delegation in a sentence. The day closed: what got done, what moved, tomorrow in order. The principal sees the problem the morning it starts.
end: That is the story. Two calls, one recap, a handful of taps. Everything on one record. Nothing sent, signed or published without a tap. What it takes to build is on the Integrations page: the phone line and transcription first, then permissions and the audit log. Those two decide whether the rest is possible.
